content.comment_body: I am using [article_no] hardware to manage temperature controls, with triggers set via an HMI panel. The system is backed up by a UPS, but it occasionally and unpredictably erases my high and low trigger values, resetting everything to zero. After installing the UPS, I realized [article_no] doesn't have retentive variables, and the HMI panel doesn't assist with retaining them. This issue has escalated and is now a major problem for me. Has anyone else experienced random erasure of variables, and does a solution exist for this?

Hello, Refer to the attached image for instructions on using retentive functionality in your blocks. You might consider using a latching relay block to help retain bit states. To check if your hardware detects any dips in power, connect the M8 bit to a counter block and make sure the retentive option is active. Testing this in simulation will show the counter increasing each time a simulated 'power cut' occurs. If you share part of your program, further advice could be provided. Greetings, [user_name].

Hello again, Upon further consideration, I suspect the problem may not be related to power interruptions. My earlier suggestion about logging power cuts still stands—see the attached image for reference. Ensure you use the M8 bit, as it is a special diagnostic tool. This approach will help confirm whether the issue stems from power cuts. Good luck. [user_name]

Thank you. Following your suggestion, I've incorporated the M8 flag connected to a counter for data logging. I've also attached a program snippet. Initially, I thought variable wipes from the HMI panel were caused by frequent power outages, but recently it happened twice without any power disturbances. Sometimes the issue remains absent for weeks. Thanks again for your help.

To be honest, I'm unsure about the exact cause. Let me offer some suggestions. When I design my programs, I implement code specifically to monitor issues—typically using timers (TOF) and counters for rapid signals. These checkpoints help detect potential errors. I recommend setting up similar checks, as illustrated in the provided example image. For systems using long-distance signals (digital, analog, communication), I suggest incorporating TON blocks to filter out sporadic signals—timers don't need to be lengthy, just sufficient to prevent quick interruptions from impacting your functions. Also, consider adding a 'health' bit sourced from the remote panel connection. My intuition points to the remote link as the problem. Placing counters at each critical junction (such as signal inputs to blocks like B021 and B24) and enabling RETENTIVE mode will help narrow down trouble spots. Please update us with your progress. If anyone else has advice, please share. Regards, [user_name]

[user_name], I added the M8 flag and additional checks as you advised. After some investigation, I discovered the issue wasn't tied to main power outages tracked by the flags. Instead, it was due to an overheated voltage converter whose faulty internal fan caused the unit to temporarily shut down and restart, erasing all user input from the HMI panel. The fix was straightforward once identified. Thanks again for your support.

No star rating? [smile]—just joking! Seriously, I greatly appreciate your feedback and am glad to hear the issue is resolved. Please visit often and continue sharing your insights with the community. Warm regards, [user_name]

analysis.insight_summary: The user encountered unexpected data loss and variable resets on their [article_no] device, which interfered with temperature management. Initial suspicion fell on power-related issues, but through diagnostic suggestions and monitoring (using retentive bits and counters), the root cause was found to be an overheating voltage converter resetting the system. The process revealed gaps in understanding of retentive memory and highlighted how hardware reliability, including power and communication, can affect system performance and troubleshooting complexity.
analysis.user_expectations: The user anticipates reliable retention of variable data despite power disruptions and expects the system to operate without unexpected resets or data loss.
